title: Chapter 16
paragraphs: Vronsky had never known anything like a real home life. His mother had been in her youth a brilliant society woman who had had during her marriage, and still more afterwards, many love affairs notorious throughout the fashionable world. His father he hardly remembered, and he had been educated in the Corps of Pages.

Leaving the school very young as a brilliant officer, he had at once entered the circle of wealthy Petersburg military men. Although he did go now and then into Petersburg society, his love affairs had always until now taken place outside it.

In Moscow, for the first time, after his luxurious and coarse Petersburg life, he had felt the whole charm of intimacy with a sweet and innocent girl of his own rank who cared for him. It never even crossed his mind that there could be anything wrong in his behavior toward Kitty. At balls he danced principally with her. He was a constant visitor at the house. He talked to her as people commonly talk in society — all sorts of nonsense, but nonsense to which he could not help attaching a special meaning in her case. Although he said nothing to her that he could not have said in front of everyone, he felt that she was becoming more and more dependent on him, and the more he felt this, the more he liked it, and the more tender his feeling for her grew. He did not know that his behavior toward Kitty had a definite name — that it was courting young girls with no intention of marriage, and that such courting was one of the bad practices common among brilliant young men like himself. It seemed to him that he was the first to have discovered this pleasure, and he was enjoying his discovery.

Had he been able to overhear what her parents were saying that evening — had he been able to step inside the family's perspective and learn that Kitty would be miserable if he did not marry her — he would have been thoroughly astonished, and wouldn't have believed it. He couldn't accept that something that gave such great and delicate pleasure to him, and above all to her, could be wrong. Still less could he have accepted that he ought to marry.

Marriage had never presented itself to him as a possibility. He not only disliked family life, but family, and especially a husband, was, according to the views general in the bachelor world in which he lived, conceived of as something alien, repulsive, and, above all, ridiculous.

But although Vronsky had not the slightest suspicion of what the parents were saying, he felt, on coming away from the Shtcherbatskys', that the secret spiritual bond between him and Kitty had grown so much stronger that evening that some step had to be taken. But what step could and should be taken, he could not imagine.

"What is so exquisite," he thought as he left the Shtcherbatskys', carrying away with him, as he always did, a delicious feeling of purity and freshness — partly because he had not been smoking for a whole evening — and with it a new feeling of tenderness at her love for him — "what is so exquisite is that not a word has been said by either of us, but we understand each other so well in this unseen language of looks and tones, that this evening more clearly than ever she told me she loves me. And how secretly, simply, and, above all, how trustfully. I feel better, purer. I feel I have a heart, and that there is a great deal of good in me. Those sweet, loving eyes! When she said: 'Indeed I do...'
"Well, what then? Oh, nothing. It's good for me, and good for her." And he started wondering where to finish the evening.

He ran through in his mind the places he might go. "Club? A game of bezique, champagne with Ignatov? No, I won't go. _Château des Fleurs_? I'll find Oblonsky there, songs, the cancan. No, I'm sick of it. That's why I like the Shtcherbatskys' — I'm growing better. I'll go home." He went straight to his room at Dussots' Hotel, ordered supper, undressed, and as soon as his head touched the pillow fell into a sound sleep.
